cim: How a Kentucky man won a religious exemption from using AI at work - The Courier-Journal
cim_eredeti: How a Kentucky man won a religious exemption from using AI at work - The Courier-Journal
szoveg_eredeti:
A University of Kentucky employee has been granted a religious exemption from using artificial intelligence in the workplace – based on his secular worldview.

David Durman is a research administrator at UK, who helps researchers at the university apply for grants. He is also a humanist, which he defines as a collection of beliefs "centered around the promotion of human wellbeing and flourishing."

Humanism is a "progressive, non-theistic belief system," according to the American Humanist Association, meaning that humanists don't believe in or don't focus on a god. But some may still consider humanism a religion, if they define religion as an ethical framework or community.

Earlier in 2026, Durman requested an exemption from using AI in his job under Title VII, which makes it illegal for employers to discriminate against employees based on religion, race, sex, color or national origin. He had not been required to use AI by his employer but said he wanted to safeguard against that possibility in the future. The technology was increasingly mentioned by Durman's colleagues and at conferences.

"There was a lot of noise, I suppose, in the work environment around it," he said. "And so pursuing the exemption was really me trying to be proactive before the environment changed to where it became the requirement – simply so I wouldn't then pursue an exemption and seem disingenuous after the fact."

Durman's exemption comes after Pope Leo XIV warned about the dehumanizing effects of AI and urged regulation of the technology in his first major document as head of the Catholic Church.

A spokesperson for UK said it reviews requests for religious accommodations on an individual basis, "considering an employee's sincerely held beliefs, essential job responsibilities and the circumstances of the request."

"In this case, the university determined that an accommodation could be provided while allowing the employee to continue performing the essential functions of their position. As technology and job responsibilities evolve, accommodations may be reviewed to ensure they remain reasonable and workable," spokesperson Jay Blanton said in a statement to the Courier Journal.

Durman became interested in philosophy as a teenager, he said, reading classic and modern philosophical texts and later taking college courses. He identified with some tenets of humanism before discovering the term.

Moral and mental development is a key component to humanism, Durman said, "but the focus is on promoting wellbeing, not only for the individual, but for your family, your community or humanity as a whole."

"That is the greatest moral pursuit," he said.

Artificial intelligence runs counter to those pursuits, he argued. An important component of humanism for Durman is the ability to take ownership of his decisions and reflect on his decision-making process. Indeed, the American Humanist Association lists critical thinking and ethical development as two of its key values.

"Offloading parts of my cognitive workload [to AI] is detrimental inherently," he said. Using the technology hampers his ability to make moral decisions, be aware of the world around him and determine what's true and not true, Durman said.

"If I'm not in command of my own mind, then everything else falls apart," he said.

The topic had been on Durman's mind for several months before he heard about a member of the Unitarian Universalist Church who secured a similar religious exemption. After that, he reached out to the American Humanist Association for help in the process, which took roughly a month after he submitted a letter to the university in late August. Durman met with UK's Office of Equal Opportunity to discuss his beliefs, and the accommodation was granted on Sept. 25.

While Durman said he thought about simply asking not to use artificial intelligence in his work, he felt that because of UK's AI pursuits, requesting an exemption through "official channels" would be cleaner and more direct. Still, he said he's "more than happy" with how UK handled his request, adding the university has always been inclusive.

Since Durman's request was granted, the American Humanist Association has seen a boost in interest surrounding religious exemptions and AI use at work, according to Alexandria Huiskens, an attorney for the organization.

And at UK, Durman said he's received emails from other members of the campus, encouraging Durman and expressing support for his efforts.

"I'm not trying to tell people how to feel about the issue," Durman said. "But my hope is if other people have concerns about [AI], to start thinking about them and bringing them forward."

Kathryn Muchnick covers children and education. Reach her at kmuchnick@usatodayco.com.
